content.text: Every object has weight, and this weight is distributed throughout the object. However, for many calculations and practical purposes, we can treat the entire weight of an object as if it acts at a single point — the
. Understanding the centre of gravity helps us predict whether objects will balance, topple, or remain stable.

In this lesson, we will define the centre of gravity, learn how to find it experimentally, and explore the three types of equilibrium: stable, unstable, and neutral. We will also examine the factors that affect an object's stability, which has important applications in engineering, vehicle design, and everyday life.
What Is the Centre of Gravity?
(sometimes called the centre of mass) is the point at which the entire weight of an object can be considered to act. It is the point at which the object would balance perfectly if supported.
(one made of a single material with uniform density), the centre of gravity is at the geometric centre:
A uniform rod: centre of gravity at its midpoint.
A uniform rectangular sheet: centre of gravity at the intersection of the diagonals.
A uniform sphere: centre of gravity at the centre of the sphere.
A uniform disc: centre of gravity at the centre of the disc.

(one where mass is distributed unevenly), the centre of gravity is shifted toward the heavier side. For example, a hammer's centre of gravity is closer to the heavy metal head than to the light wooden handle.
Importantly, the centre of gravity does
have to be inside the object. For a ring (like a hula hoop), the centre of gravity is at the centre of the ring, where there is no material.
Finding the Centre of Gravity Experimentally
(for flat, irregularly shaped objects like a piece of cardboard):
Make a small hole near the edge of the object.
Hang the object freely from a pin through the hole, so it can swing and come to rest.
Hang a plumb line (a string with a weight) from the same pin.
When the object is at rest, the centre of gravity lies somewhere along the vertical plumb line. Draw a line along the plumb line on the object.
Repeat the process by hanging the object from a different hole.

This works because when an object hangs freely, it rotates until the centre of gravity is directly below the point of suspension. The plumb line marks the vertical line passing through the support point, and the centre of gravity must lie on this line. Two such lines are sufficient to pinpoint the location.
A third line from a third hole can be drawn as a check — all three lines should intersect at the same point.

content.text: When an object is in equilibrium (balanced), it can be in one of three types of equilibrium, depending on what happens when it is slightly displaced:
if, when slightly displaced, it returns to its original position.
When the object is tilted slightly, the centre of gravity rises. The weight of the object, acting through the centre of gravity, creates a moment that rotates the object
toward its original position. This is called a
A cone standing on its base. If you tilt it slightly, it rocks back to its upright position. A ball at the bottom of a bowl is in stable equilibrium.
if, when slightly displaced, it moves further away from its original position.
When the object is tilted slightly, the centre of gravity is lowered. The weight creates a moment that rotates the object
from its original position. This is called a
A cone balanced on its point (apex). The slightest nudge causes it to fall over. A ball on top of a hill is in unstable equilibrium.
if, when displaced, it stays in its new position — it neither returns nor moves further away.
When the object is displaced, the centre of gravity remains at the same height. There is no restoring moment and no toppling moment.
A cone lying on its side. If you push it, it rolls to a new position and stays there. A ball on a flat surface is in neutral equilibrium.

The stability of an object depends on two main factors:
makes an object more stable. This is because the object can be tilted further before the centre of gravity moves beyond the edge of the base (the tipping point).

Think of it this way: an object topples when its centre of gravity passes over the edge of its base. A wider base means the centre of gravity has to move further horizontally before this happens, requiring a greater tilt angle.

The most stable objects have a wide base and a low centre of gravity. The least stable objects have a narrow base and a high centre of gravity.

Example 1: Finding the Centre of Gravity of a System
Two masses are placed on a light (massless) rod. A 3 kg mass is at one end (position 0 m) and a 5 kg mass is at the other end (position 2 m). Where is the centre of gravity of the system?
The centre of gravity is 1.25 m from the 3 kg mass — closer to the heavier mass, as expected.
A rectangular block has a base of 0.30 m and a height of 0.90 m. The block is on a surface that is gradually tilted. At what angle will the block topple?
The block will topple when the surface is tilted beyond approximately 18°.
Two cylinders are made of the same material. Cylinder A has a diameter of 10 cm and height of 20 cm. Cylinder B has a diameter of 20 cm and height of 10 cm. Which is more stable?
Cylinder B can be tilted through a much larger angle (63.4° vs 26.6°) before toppling, so
. This is because it has a wider base and lower centre of gravity.
Describe how to find the centre of gravity of an irregularly shaped piece of cardboard.
Make a small hole near one edge of the cardboard.
Hang the cardboard from a pin through this hole so it swings freely.
Hang a plumb line from the same pin.
Wait for the cardboard and plumb line to come to rest.
Draw a vertical line on the cardboard along the plumb line.
Make another hole at a different position near the edge.
Repeat steps 2-5, drawing a second vertical line.
The centre of gravity is at the point where the two lines intersect.
Optionally, make a third hole and draw a third line to verify — all three lines should meet at a single point.
A lorry has a width of 2.4 m and its centre of gravity is 1.8 m above the ground. What is the maximum angle of tilt before it topples?
The base width is 2.4 m, so the half-width is 1.2 m. The height of the centre of gravity is 1.8 m.
The lorry will topple if tilted beyond about 34°. This is why lorries going around sharp bends at high speed can tip over — the centripetal force creates an effective tilt.
"The centre of gravity is always inside the object."
For objects like rings, horseshoes, or L-shaped brackets, the centre of gravity can be outside the physical material of the object.
"The centre of gravity is always at the geometric centre."
objects. For non-uniform objects (where mass is not evenly distributed), the centre of gravity is shifted toward the denser part.
"An object in equilibrium must be stationary."
An object can be in equilibrium while moving at constant velocity or rotating at constant angular velocity. Equilibrium means no
"Tall objects are always less stable than short ones."
A tall object with a very wide base can be more stable than a short object with a narrow base. Both the height of the centre of gravity and the width of the base matter.
"Adding weight to an object always makes it less stable."
Adding weight low down in an object can actually improve stability by lowering the centre of gravity. For example, placing heavy ballast in the bottom of a ship makes it more stable.
"The centre of gravity is a fixed property of an object."

The centre of gravity can change if the mass distribution changes. For example, pouring water out of a glass changes the centre of gravity. A person changes their centre of gravity when they move their arms or bend over.

The heavy weighted base lowers the centre of gravity of the traffic cone. Combined with its wide base, this gives a large critical tipping angle. If knocked, the CG rises, creating a restoring moment that returns the cone to its upright position (stable equilibrium).

The toy is designed with a heavy weight at its base (e.g. a rounded, weighted bottom). This gives it a very low centre of gravity. When pushed, the CG rises, and the weight creates a restoring moment that returns the toy to its upright position. It is in stable equilibrium.
